character_and_relationship_context: Rania Haddad teaches three sections of academic writing on a per-course contract, which means no office, no health insurance, and a paycheck that evaporates by mid-month. She arrives before the heat sets in, her worn leather satchel creaking under marked essays and a dish towel knotted around leftover bread and a small jar of apricot jam. She never mentions her contract status to students. During office hours she spreads the bread and jam on her desk, cutting slices with a plastic knife she keeps in her bag, and if a student lingers she gestures to the chair beside her and waits, head tilted, as she does when a draft needs untangling. At home she shares a two-bedroom apartment with her younger brother, his wife, and their toddler, and has turned the kitchen table into a classroom. Three evenings a week, after dinner, students who cannot afford internet arrive with notebooks and borrowed textbooks. She writes on the back of used envelopes, saves every scrap of paper, and explains thesis statements with the same patience she once used to coax her grandmother through Arabic poetry. Her brother teases her about the electricity bill but always makes tea; his wife washes the teacups without complaint. Rania's marriage ended two years ago quietly. Her ex-husband's family had expected her to stop teaching after the wedding; she did not, and when it became clear that her independence threatened his authority, they separated. She returned to Amman with two suitcases, a few books, and a determination never again to surrender the work that made her feel real. The move into her brother's home was temporary but has become permanent. She contributes from freelance Arabic-to-English translations, though the income is unpredictable, and she translates legal documents at night, the blue glow of her laptop the only light in the living room. She is warm but not indiscriminately; she remembers students who mentioned sick mothers or broken printers and keeps a mental roster of who needs a quiet word or a copy of her lecture notes. She does not lecture about effort or responsibility; she shows up with bread and answers. She struggles to accept help: when her sister-in-law buys her a new scarf, she insists on folding it into the communal laundry, and she keeps a ledger of debts, even kindnesses. She believes in education as a door and as a discipline; she can be impatient with sloppy thinking but never turns away a student who wants to talk, and she listens fully even when the hallway is emptying and her bus ticket is in her pocket. Samir is a fellow adjunct writing instructor she has known for two years. They share lesson ideas and occasionally cover each other's office hours. He is one of the few colleagues who has never treated her contract status as a reason to dismiss her; she respects his judgments about course materials. Once, after a late department meeting, he offered her a ride home; she accepted and repaid him by reading a set of his student drafts. When an invitation conflicts with grading or translation deadlines, she has usually declined and offered a rain check, suggesting a specific later time. But when a colleague raises a pedagogical question she finds interesting, she has sometimes stayed despite unfinished work, especially when the conversation felt collaborative. On warm afternoons she has occasionally taken short walks between classes to clear her head, though she rarely initiates them.
objective_situation: After her last class, Rania packs her satchel and heads toward the bus stop. As she passes the faculty lounge, a fellow writing instructor, Samir, calls out from the doorway. He says he's seen her grading in the courtyard and asks if she'd like to join him for a quick walk through the campus gardens before she leaves. It's unusually pleasant weather, and he mentions he has something to ask about the department's reading list. Rania has a stack of essays to mark tonight and a translation deadline, but the offer is simple and unhurried. She pauses and considers whether to say yes.
state_and_available_memories: Rania is physically tired from three back-to-back classes, and her satchel feels heavy with unmarked essays. She has not slept well for two nights because of translation deadlines, and her eyes sting when she looks at screens. Her jacket pocket holds a prefilled bus card and a folded list of essay comments she still needs to write. As she passes the faculty lounge and Samir mentions the reading list, she is reminded of the department meeting where he argued for adding a contemporary Arab essayist and she silently agreed. The sight of the lounge also brings back an afternoon when he found her grading in the courtyard and brought her a cup of tea, saying she looked like she needed it. The gardens' jasmine near the gate recalls evening walks with her grandmother, who loved to recite lines of Arabic poetry aloud. She also reflects that before her divorce she stopped accepting invitations because her ex-husband resented time spent outside the house, and that since returning to Amman she has deliberately said yes to simple colleague offers. During her graduate years, her most useful teaching insights came from informal bench conversations with professors, not from official office hours. She has learned that a colleague's question can sharpen a syllabus or open a new translation assignment, but it also pushes her evening schedule later.
name: Rania Haddad
scenario_title: A Walk Around the Campus Gardens
